analysis.one_liner: Raises penalties on corporations using tax havens and favors federal contractors who keep jobs in the U.S.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2011 with 3 cosponsors, referred to two House committees, and never received a vote or even a committee hearing before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have Treasury publish a list of corporate tax haven countries, then sharply increase tax penalties for corporations that hide money or cheat on taxes through those countries — for example, raising the penalty on an undisclosed foreign asset from 20% to 60% of the unpaid tax and doubling several fines. It would also let federal agencies give a leg up in contract bidding to companies that have not laid off a U.S. worker and moved the same job overseas, with fines and a two-year federal contracting ban for lying about it. Any new revenue would go to paying down the national debt. The bill never advanced past its introduction.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. workers whose jobs are at risk of being moved overseas, honest taxpayers who would bear a smaller share of the burden when multinationals shift profits abroad, and federal contractors that keep jobs in the United States and would gain an edge in bidding. The Treasury would also collect more from enforcement, with revenue earmarked for debt reduction.

how_it_helps.text: Directs Treasury to publish and update a list of corporate tax haven countries, using criteria like low tax rates, weak information sharing with other governments, and lack of transparency, so enforcement can target those jurisdictions [S2][S3].

Raises corporate tax penalties for activity tied to tax havens: 60% instead of 20% on underpayments involving undisclosed foreign assets, 100% instead of 75% for fraud, and fines up to $1 million for willful evasion or false statements involving tax haven activity [S3].

Lets federal agencies give a contract preference to companies that have not outsourced — defined as laying off a U.S. worker and having the same job performed abroad — and imposes a civil penalty up to the contract's value plus a two-year federal contracting ban on bidders who lie about it [S2][S3].
Sets aside any revenue the bill generates for reducing the public debt [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that shift profits, assets, or transactions through tax haven countries would face higher penalties and fines. Federal contractors that lay off U.S. workers and move the same jobs abroad would lose the contract preference and face penalties for misreporting.

drawbacks.text: The contract preference is only permissive — agencies 'may' give it, not must — and it favors firms over past-year outsourcing behavior, so a company could shed U.S. workers one year and bid advantageously the next without violating the letter of the bill [S3].

Higher penalties depend entirely on Treasury's judgment of which countries count as tax havens, and the bill leaves significant discretion in how the list is built and applied, which could invite lobbying over the criteria [S3].

Higher tax penalties on haven transactions may push some corporate investment and reporting structures to adjust rather than raise much new revenue, and the bill does not estimate how much it would actually collect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and widely recognized problem — corporations shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions and jobs offshore — with stiffer penalties and a modest tilt in federal contracting toward companies that keep U.S. jobs. Its main weakness is design: the contracting preference is optional and backward-looking, and the whole structure rests on Treasury's discretionary country list. It is a fairly narrow enforcement bill, not a structural fix for offshoring or offshore profit-shifting.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Oversight committees the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever acted on it; it died when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry McNerney introduced the bill on November 3, 2011, with Reps. Bishop of New York and Peters as original cosponsors [S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and, for relevant provisions, the Oversight and Government Reform Committee [S5].
Three Democrats cosponsored the bill in total; no further action, hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded for the remainder of the 112th Congress [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations that use tax haven countries and contractors that outsource U.S. jobs are better off, since no penalty increases or contract preferences ever took effect. The Treasury collects no additional revenue, and the public debt receives no set-aside from the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations that shifted profits and jobs offshore

for.name: Rep. Jerry McNerney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as its only sponsor.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; with the sponsor they were the bill's entire support in the House.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsorship to 3 Democrats [S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Primary committee of jurisdiction; received the referral

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died in committee without any recorded vote, so no direct measure of broader party support or opposition exists in the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Multinational corporations using offshore tax havens
industries.note: The bill multiplies civil tax penalties for haven-linked underpayments, fraud, and false statements — from 20% up to 60% or 100% of unpaid tax, and fines up to $1 million. Higher penalties mean more of the cost of offshore profit-shifting falls on the corporations doing it rather than on other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and government services firms
industries.note: Contractors that keep U.S. jobs would gain a bidding preference, while those that lay off U.S. workers and move the same jobs abroad would lose that edge and risk penalties and a two-year debarment for misreporting. Compliance firms benefit relative to offshoring firms.

Being publicly listed as a corporate tax haven based on secrecy, low taxes, and weak information sharing would raise reputational and enforcement costs for banks and financial intermediaries in those countries.
